Milestones in printing technology.Diamond Sutra woodblock print: Found sealed in a cave at Dunhuang in 1900, this scroll is the oldest dated printed book known. It is now kept in the British Library.
Milestones in printing technology.Bi Sheng's movable type: Bi Sheng, a commoner under the Song dynasty, carved characters in baked clay. We know of him only because the scholar Shen Kuo wrote about it.
Milestones in printing technology.Jikji (metal type, Korea): Printed by the Korean monk Baegun, this Buddhist text is the oldest surviving book made with movable metal type, and it sits in a Paris library.
Milestones in printing technology.Gutenberg Bible: About 180 copies were printed, and fewer than 50 survive in whole or part. A complete one is among the most valuable books in the world.
Milestones in printing technology.Caxton's press in Westminster: William Caxton set up England's first press near Westminster Abbey and went on to print Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, among about a hundred titles.
Milestones in printing technology.Steam-powered press: The Times of London used Friedrich Koenig's steam press in 1814, printing over a thousand sheets an hour, several times faster than by hand.
Milestones in printing technology.Rotary printing press: Richard Hoe wrapped type around a spinning cylinder. Later versions fed from huge paper rolls, making cheap mass-circulation newspapers possible.
Milestones in printing technology.Linotype machine: Ottmar Mergenthaler's machine cast a whole line of type as one metal slug, hence the name 'line o' type'. Newspapers used it for about eighty years.
Milestones in printing technology.Xerography (photocopying): Chester Carlson made the first copy, the words '10-22-38 Astoria', in a small lab in Queens, New York. Early investors found it unimpressive.
Milestones in printing technology.Laser printer: Gary Starkweather at Xerox PARC, working around 1970, bent a laser beam to draw on a copier drum, the idea behind every office laser printer.

Tour de France winners, by first victory.Gino Bartali: Bartali won in 1938 and again in 1948, the longest gap between Tour wins. In World War II he secretly carried forged documents to help Jews escape.
Tour de France winners, by first victory.Fausto Coppi: Coppi was the first rider to win both the Giro d'Italia and the Tour de France in the same year, which he achieved in 1949.
Tour de France winners, by first victory.Jacques Anquetil: In 1957 Anquetil began a run that made him the first five-time Tour winner. He was known for his smooth time-trial style.
Tour de France winners, by first victory.Eddy Merckx: Known as 'The Cannibal' for his greed for victory, Merckx won five Tours and took the yellow, green and polka dot jerseys in 1969.
Tour de France winners, by first victory.Bernard Hinault: Nicknamed 'The Badger' for his fierce temper, Hinault won five Tours, equaling Anquetil and Merckx.
Tour de France winners, by first victory.Greg LeMond: The first American winner, LeMond took the 1989 Tour by eight seconds, the smallest margin in the race's history.
Tour de France winners, by first victory.Miguel Indurain: Indurain won five Tours in a row, from 1991 to 1995, and was famous for a resting heart rate said to be near 30 beats per minute.
Tour de France winners, by first victory.Marco Pantani: Nicknamed 'Il Pirata' for his bandana and earring, the climber won the Giro and the Tour in the same year, 1998.
Tour de France winners, by first victory.Alberto Contador: His 2010 Tour title was later stripped over a doping ban, but Contador won the Tour in 2007 and 2009.
Tour de France winners, by first victory.Chris Froome: Froome was born in Kenya and rode for Great Britain. He won four Tours between 2013 and 2017.

Length of the playing surface.Table tennis table: A full-size table is 2.74 metres long, small enough to fit indoors, and the sport's ball can be hit at over 100 km/h.
Length of the playing surface.Badminton court: Badminton shuttlecocks can reach speeds above 400 km/h in smashes, making it the fastest racket sport in terms of projectile speed.
Length of the playing surface.Volleyball court: Volleyball was invented in 1895 by William G. Morgan as a gentler alternative to basketball.
Length of the playing surface.Tennis court: Tennis courts have the same dimensions for grass, clay and hard courts, but the surfaces change how the ball bounces.
Length of the playing surface.Basketball court (FIBA): Basketball was invented in 1891 by James Naismith, who first used peach baskets as hoops.
Length of the playing surface.Netball court: Netball evolved from early basketball, and players cannot run with the ball once they have caught it.
Length of the playing surface.Olympic swimming pool: Olympic pools are 50 metres long and at least two metres deep, and have 10 lanes in modern competition.
Length of the playing surface.NHL ice rink: The rink's surface is surrounded by boards, and its corners are rounded, with the sport's players reaching speeds around 30 mph.
Length of the playing surface.NFL field with end zones: The field is 100 yards between the goal lines, plus two 10-yard end zones, and that is how it reaches this length.
Length of the playing surface.Polo field: Polo is played on horseback on one of the largest fields in sport, and players switch horses between periods.

Crypto history.Bitcoin whitepaper: Satoshi Nakamoto's nine-page paper circulated on 31 October 2008, amid the financial crisis, and the author's identity remains unknown.
Crypto history.Bitcoin genesis block: Block zero embeds a Times of London headline about a bank bailout, a timestamp and a comment.
Crypto history.Bitcoin pizza purchase: On 22 May 2010, Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoin for two pizzas, now celebrated as Bitcoin Pizza Day.
Crypto history.Silk Road shut down: The FBI shut down the dark-web market and arrested its founder Ross Ulbricht in October 2013.
Crypto history.Mt. Gox collapse: Once handling most bitcoin trade, it lost hundreds of thousands of bitcoin and filed for bankruptcy in Tokyo in early 2014.
Crypto history.Ethereum launch: Vitalik Buterin proposed it when he was 19, and the network launched in July 2015 with programmable smart contracts.
Crypto history.The DAO hack: An attacker drained about $50 million worth of ether from a crowd-funded fund, leading to a controversial blockchain fork.
Crypto history.CryptoKitties craze: The collectible-cat game clogged the Ethereum network in December 2017, and one kitten sold for over $100,000.
Crypto history.Beeple's $69M NFT sale: Everydays: The First 5000 Days sold at Christie's in March 2021, a collage of daily images.
Crypto history.FTX collapse: Founder Sam Bankman-Fried was convicted of fraud in 2023 after the exchange collapsed in November 2022.

Runes of the Elder Futhark, in order.Fehu: The name means cattle, which in the Viking world stood for wealth, and it gives the first letter of the futhark.
Runes of the Elder Futhark, in order.Uruz: Its name means aurochs, the huge wild ox that roamed Europe, now extinct.
Runes of the Elder Futhark, in order.Thurisaz: Its name means giant or thorn, and it became the thorn letter, Þ, in Old English and Icelandic.
Runes of the Elder Futhark, in order.Ansuz: The name means god, specifically Odin, and the rune is associated with speech.
Runes of the Elder Futhark, in order.Raidho: Its name means ride or journey, and it became the Latin letter R.
Runes of the Elder Futhark, in order.Gebo: Meaning gift, it is a simple X shape, and it looks like a letter that is symmetrical.
Runes of the Elder Futhark, in order.Hagalaz: Its name means hail, and the rune looks like a fence with a crossbar.
Runes of the Elder Futhark, in order.Isa: This is the simplest rune, a single vertical line, and its name means ice.
Runes of the Elder Futhark, in order.Tiwaz: Named after the god Tyr, its arrow shape fits a war god, and Tuesday is named after him.
Runes of the Elder Futhark, in order.Mannaz: Its name means human being, and it is linked to the English word man.

When these typefaces were designed.Garamond: Named for a Parisian punchcutter, it is popular for book text and was once Apple's corporate font.
When these typefaces were designed.Caslon: William Caslon's type was used for the 1776 printing of the Declaration of Independence by Dunlap and became England's default.
When these typefaces were designed.Baskerville: John Baskerville's crisp, high-contrast type was criticised by rivals who said it would blind readers.
When these typefaces were designed.Bodoni: Giambattista Bodoni's elegant high-contrast type from Parma remains a favourite of fashion magazines.
When these typefaces were designed.Futura: Paul Renner's geometric sans-serif, built on circles and triangles, is on the plaque left on the Moon by Apollo 11.
When these typefaces were designed.Times New Roman: The Times of London commissioned it from Stanley Morison and Victor Lardent to make the newspaper look sharper.
When these typefaces were designed.Helvetica: Swiss designers made it for neutrality, and a 2007 documentary celebrated its 50th anniversary.
When these typefaces were designed.Arial: Microsoft chose it as a metric-compatible alternative to Helvetica, saving licensing fees.
When these typefaces were designed.Comic Sans: Vincent Connare designed it for a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob, and it has become a favourite target of ridicule.
When these typefaces were designed.Calibri: Lucas de Groot designed it, and Microsoft made it the Office default in 2007 before replacing it with Aptos in 2023.

Tour de France climbs by summit height.La Planche des Belles Filles: Its name means plank of the beautiful girls, and Chris Froome won there in 2012 when it first became a Tour finish.
Tour de France climbs by summit height.Puy de Dome: The extinct volcano is where Anquetil and Poulidor famously duelled elbow to elbow in 1964.
Tour de France climbs by summit height.Col d'Aubisque: This Pyrenean pass has a stretch where the road clings to a cliff edge and passes through tunnels.
Tour de France climbs by summit height.Alpe d'Huez: Its 21 hairpin bends are numbered, each named for a Tour stage winner, and Dutch fans pack the corner nicknamed for them.
Tour de France climbs by summit height.Mont Ventoux: The Giant of Provence has a bare, moon-like summit, and British rider Tom Simpson died here in 1967.
Tour de France climbs by summit height.Col de la Madeleine: It is a long Alpine climb in Savoie, a regular Tour challenge before the highest passes.
Tour de France climbs by summit height.Col du Tourmalet: It is the Tour's most-climbed Pyrenean pass, first crossed in 1910.
Tour de France climbs by summit height.Col d'Izoard: Its Casse Deserte is a moonscape of rock and holds a memorial to Coppi and Bobet.
Tour de France climbs by summit height.Col du Galibier: First climbed by the Tour in 1911, this legendary pass is often cut off by snow, and its summit has a tunnel.
Tour de France climbs by summit height.Col de l'Iseran: The highest paved mountain pass in the Alps, it was first crossed by the Tour in 1938.

Famous animals of science, by their big.Clever Hans debunked: The horse seemed able to do arithmetic but was really reading unconscious cues from his questioners, a trap now called the Clever Hans effect.
Famous animals of science, by their big.Morgan's white-eyed fruit fly: Thomas Hunt Morgan spotted one white-eyed male and used it to show genes sit on chromosomes, earning a Nobel Prize in 1933.
Famous animals of science, by their big.Schrödinger's cat: Schrödinger imagined the cat, both alive and dead in a box, to point out how absurd quantum superposition seems at everyday scale; no cat was ever used.
Famous animals of science, by their big.Laika: Laika was a stray from Moscow, and she became the first animal to orbit Earth, aboard Sputnik 2.
Famous animals of science, by their big.Belka and Strelka: These Soviet dogs orbited and returned alive, and one of Strelka's puppies was given to the Kennedy family as a gift.
Famous animals of science, by their big.Ham the chimp: Ham became the first hominid in space, and he performed his lever-pulling tasks even in weightlessness.
Famous animals of science, by their big.Washoe starts learning signs: Washoe was the first chimpanzee to be taught signs from American Sign Language, and she reportedly signed to her adopted son.
Famous animals of science, by their big.Koko starts learning signs: Koko, a gorilla, reportedly used about 1,000 signs and kept pet kittens.
Famous animals of science, by their big.Alex the parrot's study begins: Alex, an African grey parrot, could name colors and shapes and showed a grasp of zero-like concepts, trained by Irene Pepperberg.
Famous animals of science, by their big.Dolly the sheep: Born at the Roslin Institute in Scotland, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell was named after Dolly Parton.

How old are these famous fossils?.Burgess Shale animals: Found by Charles Walcott in 1909 in the Canadian Rockies, its soft-bodied fossils such as Anomalocaris reveal the strange early animals of the Cambrian.
How old are these famous fossils?.Tiktaalik: Found on Canada's Ellesmere Island in 2004, this fish had a neck, a flat head and wrist-like fins, bridging fish and four-legged animals.
How old are these famous fossils?.Archaeopteryx: First found in Bavarian limestone in 1861, just two years after Darwin's Origin, it showed feathered wings alongside teeth and a long bony tail.
How old are these famous fossils?.Sue the T. rex: Named for fossil hunter Sue Hendrickson, who found her in South Dakota in 1990; she sold for $8.36 million and is now at Chicago's Field Museum.
How old are these famous fossils?.Ida (Darwinius): This young lemur-like primate from Germany's Messel Pit is so complete that even its fur outline and stomach contents survive.
How old are these famous fossils?.Toumaï (Sahelanthropus): Found in Chad in 2001, his name means 'hope of life' in the local Goran language, and his skull lay far from East Africa.
How old are these famous fossils?.Lucy: Found in Ethiopia in 1974, she was named after the Beatles song 'Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds', which was playing at camp, and she walked upright.
How old are these famous fossils?.Turkana Boy: Discovered near Lake Turkana in Kenya in 1984, this Homo erectus boy of about ten is one of the most complete early human skeletons known.
How old are these famous fossils?.Yuka the mammoth: This woolly mammoth was preserved in Siberian permafrost so well that muscle, fur and even traces of blood were found.
How old are these famous fossils?.Ötzi the Iceman: Found in the Alps on the Italian-Austrian border in 1991, he carried a copper axe, had 61 tattoos, and had been killed by an arrow.

Marie Curie's life, in order.Born in Warsaw: Born Maria Sklodowska under Russian-ruled Poland, where women could not attend university, so she studied secretly in an underground school.
Marie Curie's life, in order.Moves to Paris: She studied at the Sorbonne, living on very little in a cramped attic, and graduated at the top of her physics class in 1893.
Marie Curie's life, in order.Marries Pierre Curie: Their wedding was a plain civil ceremony with no ring, and the couple spent their honeymoon cycling through the French countryside.
Marie Curie's life, in order.Discovers polonium and radium: She named polonium after her homeland, Poland, and coined the word radioactivity.
Marie Curie's life, in order.First Nobel (Physics): Shared with Pierre and Henri Becquerel, it made her the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.
Marie Curie's life, in order.Pierre is killed: He was run over by a horse-drawn wagon on a rainy Paris street. She took over his post and became the Sorbonne's first woman professor.
Marie Curie's life, in order.Second Nobel (Chemistry): She remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences, physics and chemistry.
Marie Curie's life, in order.Mobile X-ray units in WWI: She equipped about twenty vehicles, nicknamed Little Curies, with X-ray machines, trained women to run them and drove one herself.
Marie Curie's life, in order.Tours the United States: American women raised money to buy her a gram of radium, which President Harding presented to her at the White House.
Marie Curie's life, in order.Dies: She likely died from aplastic anemia caused by radiation, and her notebooks are still radioactive and stored in lead-lined boxes.

Robotic Moon missions by launch year.Luna 2: In 1959 the Soviet probe became the first human-made object to reach the Moon, by crashing into it.
Robotic Moon missions by launch year.Ranger 7: It sent back thousands of close-up images before crashing, the first success in the Ranger program.
Robotic Moon missions by launch year.Luna 9: It made the first soft landing on the Moon and sent back panoramic photographs.
Robotic Moon missions by launch year.Lunokhod 1: It was the first remotely driven rover on another world, and ran for about 11 months.
Robotic Moon missions by launch year.Luna 24: It returned about 170 grams of lunar soil, and was the last Soviet lunar mission.
Robotic Moon missions by launch year.Clementine: The US mission hinted at water ice in polar craters, and tested sensors for the military too.
Robotic Moon missions by launch year.SMART-1: The European Space Agency's first Moon mission, powered by an ion engine.
Robotic Moon missions by launch year.Chang'e 3: It landed the Yutu rover, the first soft landing on the Moon since Luna 24 in 1976.
Robotic Moon missions by launch year.Chang'e 4: The first landing on the far side of the Moon.
Robotic Moon missions by launch year.Chandrayaan-3: India became the first country to land near the Moon's south pole.

Milestones of the motoring age.First traffic light, London: London's first signal stood outside Parliament and used gas lamps; it exploded in 1869 and injured a policeman.
Milestones of the motoring age.First speeding ticket (UK): Walter Arnold was fined for driving 8 mph in a 2 mph zone, after a policeman chased him on a bicycle.
Milestones of the motoring age.Ford's moving assembly line: The moving line cut Model T chassis assembly from over 12 hours to roughly 90 minutes.
Milestones of the motoring age.First electric traffic signal: Cleveland, Ohio installed it with red and green lights and a buzzer to warn of changes.
Milestones of the motoring age.Cologne–Bonn autobahn opens: Konrad Adenauer, then mayor of Cologne, opened it; the road had no level crossings and is often called the first autobahn.
Milestones of the motoring age.Cat's eyes road studs invented: Percy Shaw invented them in Yorkshire, reportedly inspired by light reflecting from a cat's eyes.
Milestones of the motoring age.First parking meter: Oklahoma City installed the first ones, invented by Carl Magee, to ease downtown parking congestion.
Milestones of the motoring age.UK zebra crossings arrive: Britain's striped crossings were trialed in 1951 and nicknamed 'zebra' for the black-and-white pattern.
Milestones of the motoring age.US Interstate Highway Act: President Eisenhower signed it, shaped partly by his experience of Germany's autobahns, to build about 41,000 miles of highway.
Milestones of the motoring age.Volvo three-point seat belt: Engineer Nils Bohlin designed it, and Volvo gave away the patent for other makers to use, saving countless lives.

How hot are these chili peppers?.Bell pepper: A recessive gene keeps it free of capsaicin, the compound that causes the burn. Wilbur Scoville's 1912 heat scale starts at zero with it.
How hot are these chili peppers?.Pepperoncini: The name means "little peppers" in Italian, but in the US these tangy, pickled peppers are most often served on salads and sandwiches with a Greek flavor.
How hot are these chili peppers?.Poblano: This dark green Mexican chili is stuffed with cheese for chiles rellenos. Dried, it becomes ancho, a staple of mole sauces.
How hot are these chili peppers?.Jalapeño: Named for Xalapa, Veracruz. Smoked and dried, it becomes chipotle, a staple of Mexican and Tex-Mex cooking.
How hot are these chili peppers?.Serrano: Its name comes from "sierra", as in mountains, referring to the highlands of Puebla and Hidalgo where it was first grown. Salsa cooks love it.
How hot are these chili peppers?.Cayenne: Named for the city of Cayenne in French Guiana, this long, thin red chili is typically dried and ground into the familiar spice.
How hot are these chili peppers?.Thai bird's eye: In Thai it is called "prik kee noo", meaning "mouse-dropping chili", for its small size. It packs a punch in curries and dipping sauces.
How hot are these chili peppers?.Habanero: Its name means "from Havana", though it is mostly grown in Mexico's Yucatan. It is a close cousin of the Scotch bonnet from Jamaica.
How hot are these chili peppers?.Ghost pepper: Bhut jolokia from northeast India was rated the world's hottest in 2007 by Guinness, and India's military has tested it in non-lethal grenades.
How hot are these chili peppers?.Carolina Reaper: Bred by Ed Currie in South Carolina, it held the Guinness record for the hottest chili from 2013 until 2023 and has a distinctive pointed tail.

When these toy and game makers were foun.Milton Bradley: Founded in Springfield, Massachusetts, it made The Checkered Game of Life and later the 1960s hit Twister. It was bought by Hasbro in 1984.
When these toy and game makers were foun.Steiff: The German company made the first teddy bear with moving limbs, and its signature "button in ear" is the sign of an original, since 1904.
When these toy and game makers were foun.Parker Brothers: Based in Salem, Massachusetts, it published Monopoly in 1935 and also Clue, Risk, and Sorry!, and was later bought by General Mills, then Hasbro.
When these toy and game makers were foun.Hasbro: Founded in Rhode Island by the Hassenfeld brothers, selling textile remnants first. It later made Mr. Potato Head, Transformers and My Little Pony.
When these toy and game makers were foun.Fisher-Price: Founded in New York during the Great Depression, it's known for its Little People and wooden pull toys, and for being a classic toy brand.
When these toy and game makers were foun.LEGO: The Danish company began by making wooden toys in 1932, and the name comes from "leg godt", Danish for "play well", and it later started using plastic bricks.
When these toy and game makers were foun.Mattel: Founded in a California garage by Harold "Matt" Matson and Elliot Handler, its name blends Matt and Elliot. Elliot's wife Ruth created Barbie in 1959.
When these toy and game makers were foun.Bandai: The Japanese toy and games company founded in 1950, and the maker of Gundam model kits and the brand behind games like Tekken and Pac-Man.
When these toy and game makers were foun.Playmobil figures: The tiny figures were designed by Hans Beck at the German firm Geobra Brandstatter, which dates to 1876, and launched at the 1974 Nuremberg Toy Fair.
When these toy and game makers were foun.Funko: Founded in Washington State in 1998 as a small company making bobblehead toys, it is now famous for collectible pop vinyl figures of film, TV and sports characters.

When these hot sauce brands were born.Tabasco: Made on Avery Island, Louisiana, and aged in oak barrels for years, it is still family-owned after more than 150 years.
When these hot sauce brands were born.Frank's RedHot: Its sauce was used in the original Buffalo wings at Anchor Bar, and it is the classic Buffalo wing sauce base.
When these hot sauce brands were born.Crystal: This Louisiana-style sauce is thin and vinegary, a classic splash on seafood and po' boys in New Orleans.
When these hot sauce brands were born.Texas Pete: Despite the name, it is made in North Carolina; its founders thought 'Texas' sounded spicier.
When these hot sauce brands were born.Valentina: This Mexican sauce from Guadalajara is thick and mild, and popular on fruit, chips and street snacks.
When these hot sauce brands were born.El Yucateco: Its habanero peppers are a Yucatan staple, and the name means 'the Yucatecan'; the green bottle is iconic.
When these hot sauce brands were born.Tapatío: 'Tapatio' is a nickname for people from Guadalajara, though this sauce was started in California.
When these hot sauce brands were born.Huy Fong Sriracha: David Tran, a Vietnamese refugee, put a rooster on the label because it was his birth year in the zodiac.
When these hot sauce brands were born.Cholula: It is named for an ancient city in Puebla, Mexico, and its sauce is easy to spot by its round wooden cap.
When these hot sauce brands were born.Mike's Hot Honey: Mike Kurtz made chilli-infused honey in Brooklyn, and it became a favourite pizza topping.

Gone but not forgotten: when they died o.Anomalocaris: This early predator, whose name means 'abnormal shrimp', was up to a metre long, and its fossils were first mistaken for several animals.
Gone but not forgotten: when they died o.Trilobites: These armoured sea creatures survived for about 270 million years and vanished in the greatest mass extinction.
Gone but not forgotten: when they died o.Stegosaurus: The plated herbivore lived long before T. rex, and it lived closer in time to us than to Stegosaurus.
Gone but not forgotten: when they died o.Tyrannosaurus rex: The most famous predator was wiped out when an asteroid hit what is now Mexico, ending the age of the dinosaurs.
Gone but not forgotten: when they died o.Megalodon: This huge shark could grow longer than a bus, and the teeth are large as a human hand.
Gone but not forgotten: when they died o.Neanderthals: These cousins interbred with our ancestors, and many people today carry a small percentage of their DNA.
Gone but not forgotten: when they died o.Sabre-toothed cat: Smilodon's canines were about 18 centimetres long, and it hunted in the Americas until the end of the last ice age.
Gone but not forgotten: when they died o.Woolly mammoth (last ones): A small population lived on Wrangel Island and died out around the time the pyramids were built.
Gone but not forgotten: when they died o.Dodo: This flightless pigeon was discovered by Dutch sailors on Mauritius, and it was extinct within about a century.
Gone but not forgotten: when they died o.Steller's sea cow: Discovered in 1741 and hunted to extinction within 27 years, this giant relative of the manatee grew up to eight metres long.

How many legs does it have?.Snake: Snakes evolved from legged lizards, and pythons still keep tiny leg spurs near their tails.
How many legs does it have?.Ostrich: It has just two toes on each foot, unique among birds, and can run about 70 km/h.
How many legs does it have?.Horse: Horses walk on a single enlarged toe per foot, with the hoof as the toenail.
How many legs does it have?.Ant: Ants have no lungs and breathe through tiny holes along their bodies.
How many legs does it have?.Tarantula: A tarantula can regrow a lost leg when it molts.
How many legs does it have?.Lobster: Counting its pincers, this crustacean is a decapod, meaning 'ten-footed'.
How many legs does it have?.Woodlouse: Woodlice are crustaceans, not insects, more closely related to crabs than to beetles.
How many legs does it have?.House centipede: It has 15 pairs of long legs and hunts household pests like spiders and silverfish.
How many legs does it have?.Red-headed centipede: Its 21 pairs of legs carry a fast hunter, and the first pair is modified into venomous fangs.
How many legs does it have?.Record-holding millipede: Illacme plenipes from California holds the record. Millipede means 'thousand feet' but few come close.

Water content of body tissues and fluids.Tooth enamel: The hardest substance in the body is almost entirely mineral, with very little water.
Water content of body tissues and fluids.Fat tissue: Fat repels water, and leaner people have a higher body water percentage.
Water content of body tissues and fluids.Bone: Bone is living tissue, constantly rebuilt, not a dry stick.
Water content of body tissues and fluids.Skin: It forms a waterproof barrier, which is why you don't swell up in a bath, and fingers wrinkle from nerve signals.
Water content of body tissues and fluids.Brain: The brain uses about a fifth of the body's energy while being only a small fraction of its weight.
Water content of body tissues and fluids.Muscle: Muscle is far wetter than fat, so muscular people hold more water.
Water content of body tissues and fluids.Lungs: Lungs hold about 480 million tiny air sacs.
Water content of body tissues and fluids.Blood plasma: The yellowish fluid makes up a bit over half of blood volume.
Water content of body tissues and fluids.Urine: It is mostly water with urea and salts, and its yellow color comes from urochrome.
Water content of body tissues and fluids.Vitreous humor (eye gel): Almost pure water thickened by collagen and hyaluronic acid into a clear gel.

Ottoman sultans, by accession.Osman I: The dynasty and the word Ottoman come from his name; he led a small band of Turkic warriors on the edge of Byzantine Anatolia.
Ottoman sultans, by accession.Orhan: Orhan took Bursa, the first Ottoman capital, and his son Süleyman crossed into Europe, capturing Gallipoli in 1354.
Ottoman sultans, by accession.Murad I: Murad I took Adrianople (Edirne), making it a capital, and died at the first Battle of Kosovo in 1389.
Ottoman sultans, by accession.Bayezid I: Nicknamed Yıldırım, the Thunderbolt, he was captured by Timur at the Battle of Ankara in 1402, a defeat that nearly broke the empire.
Ottoman sultans, by accession.Mehmed the Conqueror: He took Constantinople in 1453 aged 21, ending the Byzantine Empire after over a thousand years.
Ottoman sultans, by accession.Selim the Grim: In only eight years Selim conquered Syria and Egypt and gained Mecca and Medina, nearly tripling the empire's size.
Ottoman sultans, by accession.Suleiman the Magnificent: Called Kanuni, the Lawgiver, by his own people, Suleiman ruled for 46 years and the empire reached its peak in his reign.
Ottoman sultans, by accession.Selim II: Nicknamed the Sot for his love of wine, Selim II left rule to his vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha; the fleet captured Cyprus but lost at Lepanto.
Ottoman sultans, by accession.Murad IV: Murad IV banned coffee, tobacco and alcohol in his lands, reportedly with harsh penalties, and recaptured Baghdad in 1638.
Ottoman sultans, by accession.Mehmed VI: The last Ottoman sultan left Istanbul aboard a British warship in 1922, after the sultanate was abolished.

Greek letters in alphabet order.Alpha α: Alpha and omega, first and last letters, together mean the beginning and the end; the word alphabet comes from alpha plus beta.
Greek letters in alphabet order.Gamma γ: Gamma rays are the most energetic form of electromagnetic radiation, named after the third Greek letter by analogy with alpha and beta rays.
Greek letters in alphabet order.Delta δ: Delta resembles a triangle, and river deltas got their name when Herodotus described the Nile's triangular mouth.
Greek letters in alphabet order.Theta θ: Theta brain waves occur during drowsiness and deep relaxation, and mathematicians favor the letter for angles.
Greek letters in alphabet order.Lambda λ: Spartans reportedly painted it on their shields for Lacedaemon, and physicists use it for wavelength.
Greek letters in alphabet order.Mu μ: Mu stands for micro, a millionth, as in micrometer, and for the coefficient of friction in physics.
Greek letters in alphabet order.Pi π: Pi, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, never ends, and computers have calculated it to trillions of digits.
Greek letters in alphabet order.Sigma σ: In math, capital sigma means a sum, and lowercase sigma has a special form, ς, used only at the end of a word.
Greek letters in alphabet order.Phi φ: Phi stands for the golden ratio, about 1.618, said to be named after the Greek sculptor Phidias.
Greek letters in alphabet order.Omega ω: Omega means great O in Greek, as opposed to little o, omicron, and the Swiss watchmaker took the name for ultimate achievement.

Astronomy's Nobel Prizes in Physics.Pulsars (Hewish): Hewish won, but his student Jocelyn Bell Burnell, who spotted the signal, was famously left out.
Astronomy's Nobel Prizes in Physics.Discovery of the CMB: Penzias and Wilson found a persistent hiss in their Holmdel horn antenna, and first suspected pigeon droppings.
Astronomy's Nobel Prizes in Physics.Chandrasekhar's star physics: His limit of about 1.4 solar masses is the maximum mass of a stable white dwarf.
Astronomy's Nobel Prizes in Physics.Binary pulsar (Hulse, Taylor): The pair showed the binary pulsar's orbit shrinks exactly as gravitational waves predict, first indirect evidence.
Astronomy's Nobel Prizes in Physics.Cosmic neutrinos and X-rays: Davis and Koshiba detected neutrinos from the Sun and a supernova, and Giacconi found X-ray sources.
Astronomy's Nobel Prizes in Physics.COBE: the CMB's spectrum: Mather and Smoot measured the CMB's blackbody spectrum and its tiny temperature ripples.
Astronomy's Nobel Prizes in Physics.Accelerating universe: Perlmutter, Schmidt and Riess used distant supernovae to show the expansion is speeding up, implying dark energy.
Astronomy's Nobel Prizes in Physics.Gravitational waves (LIGO): Weiss, Barish and Thorne were honoured for the 2015 detection of merging black holes about 1.3 billion light-years away.
Astronomy's Nobel Prizes in Physics.First exoplanet and cosmology: Peebles won for cosmology, and Mayor and Queloz found the first planet orbiting a Sun-like star, 51 Pegasi b.
Astronomy's Nobel Prizes in Physics.Black holes (Penrose, Ghez): Penrose showed relativity predicts black holes, while Genzel and Ghez found the supermassive one at our galaxy's center.

US presidents who share a surname, in or.John Adams: Our second president died on 4 July 1826, the same day as Thomas Jefferson, fifty years after independence.
US presidents who share a surname, in or.John Quincy Adams: After his presidency he served 17 years in the House of Representatives, where he fought against the gag rule on slavery petitions.
US presidents who share a surname, in or.William Henry Harrison: His inauguration speech ran about two hours in the cold, and he died 31 days later, the shortest presidency ever.
US presidents who share a surname, in or.Andrew Johnson: The first president to be impeached, in 1868, he survived the Senate trial by a single vote.
US presidents who share a surname, in or.Benjamin Harrison: Grandson of William Henry Harrison. He won in 1888 with a majority in the Electoral College despite losing the popular vote.
US presidents who share a surname, in or.Theodore Roosevelt: The teddy bear is named after him. At age 42 he became the youngest person to serve as president.
US presidents who share a surname, in or.Franklin D. Roosevelt: The only president elected four times. The 22nd Amendment later limited presidents to two terms.
US presidents who share a surname, in or.Lyndon B. Johnson: He was sworn in aboard Air Force One after Kennedy's assassination, and signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
US presidents who share a surname, in or.George H. W. Bush: As a teenager he became one of the youngest US Navy pilots in World War II.
US presidents who share a surname, in or.George W. Bush: The second president whose father had also been president, after John Quincy Adams.

Chewing gum brands, by launch year.Juicy Fruit: William Wrigley Jr. first gave it away free with baking powder, and the fruity gum soon outsold the product it came with.
Chewing gum brands, by launch year.Doublemint: Its 'double your pleasure, double your fun' jingle and ads with twins made it one of Wrigley's best-known spearmint gums.
Chewing gum brands, by launch year.Dubble Bubble: Fleer's Walter Diemer mixed the first batch, and it turned pink because that was the only dye he had on hand.
Chewing gum brands, by launch year.Bazooka: The name came from a comedian's homemade horn, the bazooka, and every piece wraps a tiny Bazooka Joe comic strip.
Chewing gum brands, by launch year.Trident: Its ads famously said four out of five dentists surveyed recommend sugarless gum for patients who chew gum.
Chewing gum brands, by launch year.Big Red: Punchy cinnamon heat made it a cult favorite, and in the US many people still just ask for it by name.
Chewing gum brands, by launch year.Hubba Bubba: Wrigley made it as a bubble gum that wouldn't stick to your face when the bubble popped, which was its big selling point.
Chewing gum brands, by launch year.Extra: Wrigley's sugar-free pack took off as chewing gum shifted away from sugary sticks and toward breath-freshening flavors.
Chewing gum brands, by launch year.Bubble Tape: Six feet of bubble gum coiled in a tape-measure-style dispenser, made so kids could tear off as much as they wanted.
Chewing gum brands, by launch year.5 Gum: Wrigley's 5 comes in flavors named like Cobalt and Rain, and it was marketed as a sensory experience rather than a treat.

Nobel Prize in Physics: when these were.Electron (J.J. Thomson): J.J. Thomson's discovery, which proved atoms are divisible, and his son George also won a Nobel Prize for showing electrons behave as waves.
Nobel Prize in Physics: when these were.Neutron: James Chadwick discovered the particle in 1932, which explained why atoms weigh more than their protons alone.
Nobel Prize in Physics: when these were.Positron: Carl Anderson found the electron's antimatter twin in cosmic ray tracks, and it was the first antimatter ever seen.
Nobel Prize in Physics: when these were.BCS superconductivity: Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer explained superconductivity, and Bardeen became the only person to win two physics Nobels, the other for the transistor.
Nobel Prize in Physics: when these were.Pulsars: Discovered by Jocelyn Bell Burnell, the first pulsar, whose Nobel went to her supervisor, not her, a famous controversy.
Nobel Prize in Physics: when these were.Cosmic microwave background: Penzias and Wilson heard the leftover glow of the Big Bang, and the signal was the first strong evidence for it.
Nobel Prize in Physics: when these were.Graphene: Geim and Novoselov lifted single-atom-thick carbon layers with sticky tape, and the material is stronger than steel.
Nobel Prize in Physics: when these were.Neutrino oscillations: Takaaki Kajita and Arthur McDonald showed neutrinos change type, which means they have mass.
Nobel Prize in Physics: when these were.Gravitational waves: The LIGO team detected ripples in spacetime from colliding black holes, a century after Einstein predicted them.
Nobel Prize in Physics: when these were.Exoplanet around a Sun star: Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found 51 Pegasi b, a planet orbiting a Sun-like star, which was the first of thousands.

When these landmark cookbooks appeared.Apicius: Apicius is a collection of Roman recipes, and it's the oldest surviving cookbook in Latin, with dishes like flamingo tongues.
When these landmark cookbooks appeared.Le Viandier: This French medieval cookbook attributed to Taillevent, who served the French court, was copied for centuries.
When these landmark cookbooks appeared.The Forme of Cury: The scroll was compiled by cooks of Richard II, and it gives recipes for dishes like rabbit, spices and cheese.
When these landmark cookbooks appeared.Glasse's Art of Cookery: Hannah Glasse's book was a bestseller, and she is often wrongly quoted as saying 'First catch your hare', which isn't in it.
When these landmark cookbooks appeared.Simmons' American Cookery: Amelia Simmons wrote the first American cookbook, and it introduced New World ingredients like cornmeal and pumpkin.
When these landmark cookbooks appeared.Mrs Beeton's Household Mgmt: Isabella Beeton's guide was wildly popular for Victorian households, but she died at 28, shortly after its publication.
When these landmark cookbooks appeared.The Fannie Farmer Cookbook: Fannie Farmer popularized standardized level measurements in recipes, which replaced vague terms like a 'teacup' or a 'handful'.
When these landmark cookbooks appeared.Escoffier's Le Guide Culinaire: Auguste Escoffier codified French cuisine and organized kitchens into the brigade system, and also created the peach Melba.
When these landmark cookbooks appeared.Joy of Cooking: Irma Rombauer self-published it in St. Louis during the Great Depression, and it became a kitchen classic.
Julia Child co-wrote this book with Simone Beck and Louisette Bertholle, and it brought French cooking to American kitchens.

The French Revolution, in order.Estates-General convenes: The Estates-General hadn't met since 1614, and when it did, a fight over voting rules helped set off the revolution.
The French Revolution, in order.Storming of the Bastille: A crowd stormed the Bastille looking for gunpowder, and found only seven prisoners inside.
The French Revolution, in order.Rights of Man declared: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen declared that men are born free and equal, and it's still part of French law.
The French Revolution, in order.Women's March on Versailles: Thousands of Parisian women, angry over bread prices, marched to Versailles and forced the royal family back to Paris.
The French Revolution, in order.Flight to Varennes: Louis XVI and his family tried to flee but were caught at Varennes, partly because a postmaster recognized him from a coin.
The French Revolution, in order.Monarchy abolished: The monarchy was abolished and France became a republic, and the new calendar began a new year one.
The French Revolution, in order.Louis XVI guillotined: Louis XVI was executed by guillotine in Paris, after being convicted of treason by the National Convention.
The French Revolution, in order.Marie Antoinette guillotined: Marie Antoinette was guillotined nine months after her husband, and the line let them eat cake is almost certainly not hers.
The French Revolution, in order.Robespierre executed: Robespierre, the architect of the Terror, was himself guillotined, ending that bloody phase.
The French Revolution, in order.Napoleon's Brumaire coup: Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in the coup of 18 Brumaire, and he made himself First Consul, later emperor.

Pressure: from near-vacuum to crushing.Surface of the Moon: The Moon has only a trace of gas above its surface, far less than any lab on Earth. Even so, it has a very faint exosphere.
Pressure: from near-vacuum to crushing.Surface of Pluto: Pluto's thin nitrogen atmosphere freezes and falls as snow as the planet moves away from the Sun. New Horizons measured it in 2015.
Pressure: from near-vacuum to crushing.Surface of Mars: Mars's air is only about 0.6% as dense as Earth's. At this pressure, liquid water would boil away at very low temperatures.
Pressure: from near-vacuum to crushing.Summit of Everest: At the top of the world's tallest mountain, the air has about a third of the sea-level pressure. Climbers often use bottled oxygen.
Pressure: from near-vacuum to crushing.Airliner cabin: Planes are pressurised to feel like an altitude of around 2,000 m. That is why your ears pop and sealed snack bags puff up.
Pressure: from near-vacuum to crushing.Earth at sea level: The weight of air above each square metre is about ten tonnes. We don't notice because our bodies push back from inside.
Pressure: from near-vacuum to crushing.Surface of Titan: Titan's thick atmosphere is the only one in the solar system, besides Earth's, rich in nitrogen. Cassini's Huygens probe landed there in 2005.
Pressure: from near-vacuum to crushing.30 m underwater: Pressure rises by about one bar for every 10 metres of water. At 30 m, you feel four times the pressure at the surface, which is why divers use gauges.
Pressure: from near-vacuum to crushing.Surface of Venus: Venus's surface pressure is like being 900 m under the ocean. Soviet Venera probes survived there for only an hour or two.
Pressure: from near-vacuum to crushing.Mariana Trench floor: The bottom of the Challenger Deep is more than 10,900 m below the surface. The pressure is over a thousand times that at the surface.

Fat per 100 grams.Skim milk: Cream rises, so milk is skimmed by taking it off, and the milk keeps nearly all its calcium.
Fat per 100 grams.Chicken breast: Skinless chicken breast is among the leanest meats, and the skin more than doubles the fat.
Fat per 100 grams.Egg: Nearly all an egg's fat sits in the yolk; the white has almost none.
Fat per 100 grams.Avocado: Mostly heart-friendly monounsaturated fat, as in olive oil, which is unusual for a fruit.
Fat per 100 grams.Cheddar: Named after the village of Cheddar in Somerset, England, where the cheese was first made.
Fat per 100 grams.70% dark chocolate: Most of the fat is cocoa butter, which melts just below body temperature.
Fat per 100 grams.Peanut butter: Peanuts are legumes, not true nuts, and they grow underground.
Fat per 100 grams.Walnuts: They are unusually rich in plant omega-3 fat, and they are the only nut with so much.
Fat per 100 grams.Butter: Butter is about 80 percent fat, and the rest is mostly water.
Fat per 100 grams.Olive oil: Pure fat with no water, so a tablespoon holds roughly 120 calories.

Great American novels, by publication.The Jungle: Upton Sinclair's exposé of meatpacking helped bring about the Pure Food and Drug Act.
Great American novels, by publication.The Great Gatsby: Fitzgerald's novel sold modestly in his lifetime, and became a classic after his death.
Great American novels, by publication.The Sound and the Fury: Faulkner took its title from Macbeth's speech about life being a tale told by an idiot.
Great American novels, by publication.The Grapes of Wrath: Steinbeck's novel follows the Joad family out of the Dust Bowl, and won a Pulitzer.
Great American novels, by publication.The Catcher in the Rye: Holden Caulfield's narration is still widely read, and J.D. Salinger became a recluse afterward.
Great American novels, by publication.Invisible Man: Ralph Ellison's only novel in his lifetime won the 1953 National Book Award.
Great American novels, by publication.To Kill a Mockingbird: Harper Lee's novel won the Pulitzer in 1961; Atticus Finch is its moral center.
Great American novels, by publication.Catch-22: Joseph Heller's title entered dictionaries as a term for a no-win situation.
Great American novels, by publication.Slaughterhouse-Five: Vonnegut's 'So it goes' refrain follows every death.
Great American novels, by publication.Beloved: Toni Morrison's Pulitzer winner was inspired by the real story of Margaret Garner.

Meat-eaters, from tiny to colossal.Common shrew: This tiny insect-eater must eat nearly its own body weight every day or starve. It lives only about a year and a half at most.
Meat-eaters, from tiny to colossal.Least weasel: The world's smallest carnivore is slender enough to enter mouse burrows, and it hunts animals larger than itself. It turns white in snowy places.
Meat-eaters, from tiny to colossal.Kestrel: Kestrels hover in place while hunting, and they can see ultraviolet light, which helps them spot the urine trails of voles in grass.
Meat-eaters, from tiny to colossal.Peregrine falcon: In a dive, called a stoop, it can exceed 300 km/h, making it the fastest animal on Earth. It nests on city skyscrapers as well as cliffs.
Meat-eaters, from tiny to colossal.Eurasian lynx: This secretive wild cat has tufts on its ears and large padded paws that work like snowshoes. It is being reintroduced in parts of Europe.
Meat-eaters, from tiny to colossal.Grey wolf: Wolves live in family packs led by a breeding pair. All domestic dogs descend from them, and their howls can carry for many kilometres.
Meat-eaters, from tiny to colossal.Bengal tiger: No two tigers share the same stripe pattern, and the stripes go all the way into the skin. Most of India's tigers are of this subspecies.
Meat-eaters, from tiny to colossal.Polar bear: Its skin is black, and the fur is translucent, not white. It is the largest land carnivore and can smell a seal from about a kilometre away.
Meat-eaters, from tiny to colossal.Orca: Orcas are the largest dolphins and hunt in family pods with cultures of their own, including different hunting techniques and dialects.
Meat-eaters, from tiny to colossal.Sperm whale (male): The largest toothed predator hunts giant squid in the deep, diving for an hour. It has the biggest brain of any animal on Earth.

Earth and us, in percentages.Carbon dioxide in air: Although it is a tiny fraction, carbon dioxide traps heat and powers plant growth. Its level has risen sharply since the Industrial Revolution.
Earth and us, in percentages.Argon in air: The third most abundant gas in air, argon is a chemically inert noble gas. Its name comes from the Greek for lazy, since it does not react.
Earth and us, in percentages.Earth's water that's fresh: Most of the planet's water is salty ocean. Only a small sliver is fresh, and most of that is frozen or underground.
Earth and us, in percentages.Oxygen in air: Oxygen was nearly absent from early Earth's air. It built up after cyanobacteria began photosynthesis billions of years ago.
Earth and us, in percentages.Earth's surface that's land: The land is unevenly spread, with most of it in the northern hemisphere. Asia alone covers nearly a third of all land.
Earth and us, in percentages.Water in an adult body: Roughly 60 per cent of an adult's body is water, a bit less in older people. Your brain is about three quarters water.
Earth and us, in percentages.Fresh water locked in ice: Glaciers and ice sheets, mostly in Antarctica and Greenland, hold most of the world's fresh water. Only a small share runs in rivers and lakes.
Earth and us, in percentages.Earth's surface that's ocean: The oceans cover about 71 per cent of the surface, which is why Earth looks blue from space. Most of the deep seafloor is still unmapped in detail.
Earth and us, in percentages.Nitrogen in air: Nitrogen makes up most of the air, but it is mostly inert, and plants can't use it directly. Special bacteria convert it into forms they can take up.
Earth and us, in percentages.Water in a cucumber: Cucumbers are among the most watery foods and can feel cool inside even on a hot day. They belong to the same plant family as melons and squash.

Sailing from London to Tokyo via Suez.English Channel: The sea route begins as ships leave the Thames and head through this busy strait, one of the world's busiest shipping lanes, between England and France.
Sailing from London to Tokyo via Suez.Bay of Biscay: This stretch of the Atlantic off France and Spain is notorious for rough seas and big swells, and sailors have long feared its storms.
Sailing from London to Tokyo via Suez.Strait of Gibraltar: The narrow gateway between Spain and Morocco is only about 14 km wide at its narrowest. In myth, the Rock of Gibraltar was one of the Pillars of Hercules.
Sailing from London to Tokyo via Suez.Mediterranean Sea: Its name means middle of the land. It was the highway of Phoenicians, Greeks and Romans, and it is almost enclosed by land.
Sailing from London to Tokyo via Suez.Suez Canal: This waterway opened in 1869 and saves ships from sailing around Africa. In 2021 the container ship Ever Given got stuck across it, halting traffic for six days.
Sailing from London to Tokyo via Suez.Red Sea: Its name may come from seasonal algae blooms that turn the water reddish. It is known for superb coral reefs and warm, salty water.
Sailing from London to Tokyo via Suez.Gulf of Aden: This stretch between Yemen and Somalia has been plagued by pirates in recent decades, so warships often escort merchant ships through it.
Sailing from London to Tokyo via Suez.Arabian Sea: The part of the Indian Ocean between India and Arabia. For centuries traders used the monsoon winds to sail across it with the seasons.
Sailing from London to Tokyo via Suez.Strait of Malacca: A narrow channel between Malaysia and Sumatra, it is one of the busiest sea lanes in the world, and a large share of global trade passes through it.
Sailing from London to Tokyo via Suez.South China Sea: This sea is a major trade route with several nations claiming parts of it. Beyond it lie the East China Sea, the Pacific and the final approach to Japan.

When these instruments appeared.Bone flute: Flutes made of bird bone and mammoth ivory, found in Germany, are among the oldest known instruments.
When these instruments appeared.Lyres of Ur: Discovered in the Royal Cemetery of Ur by Leonard Woolley, one has a golden bull's head and lapis inlay.
When these instruments appeared.Violin: Andrea Amati of Cremona is credited with the early violin design, which Stradivari later perfected.
When these instruments appeared.Piano: Bartolomeo Cristofori invented it in Florence; its original name meant soft and loud harpsichord.
When these instruments appeared.Accordion patent: Cyrill Demian patented it in Vienna, and its name comes from the German Akkord, meaning chord.
When these instruments appeared.Saxophone patent: Adolphe Sax of Belgium patented it as a bridge between woodwind and brass.
When these instruments appeared.Theremin: It is played without touching it, and Soviet physicist Leon Theremin invented it; it's the eerie sound in sci-fi films.
When these instruments appeared.Electric guitar (Frying Pan): George Beauchamp's aluminium electric lap steel guitar was nicknamed the Frying Pan.
When these instruments appeared.Fender Stratocaster: Leo Fender's design with three pickups and a tremolo arm has been played by Hendrix and Clapton.
When these instruments appeared.Moog synthesizer: Robert Moog's modular instrument made keyboard-controlled voltage music, popularised by Switched-On Bach.

How much these dogs weigh.Chihuahua: The world's smallest breed is named for a Mexican state, and its skull has a soft spot called a molera that can persist into adulthood.
How much these dogs weigh.Pug: Chinese emperors kept them as companions, and a group of pugs is called a grumble.
How much these dogs weigh.Beagle: With about 220 million scent receptors, beagles are used at airports to sniff out food in luggage.
How much these dogs weigh.Border Collie: Widely seen as the most intelligent breed; one named Chaser learned over 1,000 words.
How much these dogs weigh.English Bulldog: Originally bred for bull-baiting, it is now a gentle companion, and a mascot for Yale and many schools.
How much these dogs weigh.Golden Retriever: Bred in 19th-century Scotland to retrieve waterfowl, it's now one of the most popular family and guide dogs.
How much these dogs weigh.Rottweiler: It is named for the German town Rottweil, where dogs drove cattle to market.
How much these dogs weigh.Great Dane: Despite the name, it came from Germany; Zeus held the record for tallest dog.
How much these dogs weigh.Saint Bernard: Named after the Great St Bernard Pass hospice; the rescue dogs reportedly never carried brandy barrels.
How much these dogs weigh.English Mastiff: Among the heaviest dogs, one named Aicama Zorba weighed about 155 kilograms in 1989.

Golden Age Islamic scholars, by birth.Al-Khwarizmi: This Baghdad mathematician's name gave us the word 'algorithm', and his book al-jabr gave us 'algebra'.
Golden Age Islamic scholars, by birth.Al-Razi: A Persian physician who distinguished smallpox from measles and ran a famous hospital, he is also known in Europe as Rhazes.
Golden Age Islamic scholars, by birth.Al-Farabi: Known as the 'Second Teacher' after Aristotle, this philosopher also wrote major works on music theory and political thought.
Golden Age Islamic scholars, by birth.Ibn al-Haytham: His Book of Optics showed that we see because light enters the eye, and he promoted testing ideas by experiment.
Golden Age Islamic scholars, by birth.Al-Biruni: He estimated Earth's radius with impressive accuracy using a mountain and trigonometry, and wrote a famous study of India.
Golden Age Islamic scholars, by birth.Avicenna: His Canon of Medicine was a standard textbook in Europe and the Islamic world for centuries; his Arabic name is Ibn Sina.
Golden Age Islamic scholars, by birth.Al-Ghazali: A theologian and philosopher who left a prestigious Baghdad post after a spiritual crisis, he shaped Sunni thought for centuries.
Golden Age Islamic scholars, by birth.Averroes: This Cordoba-born judge and philosopher wrote such influential commentaries on Aristotle that medieval Europeans simply called him 'the Commentator'.
Golden Age Islamic scholars, by birth.Ibn Battuta: A Moroccan traveler who journeyed for about thirty years across Africa and Asia, covering far more distance than Marco Polo.
Golden Age Islamic scholars, by birth.Ibn Khaldun: His Muqaddimah is a pioneering work on history, economics and society, and he is often called a founder of sociology.

Lent to Pentecost, counted from Easter.Shrove Tuesday: Known as Mardi Gras in some places, this is the day to use up rich foods like eggs and butter before Lent begins, hence pancakes.
Lent to Pentecost, counted from Easter.Ash Wednesday: Worshippers receive a cross of ashes on the forehead as Lent begins, ashes traditionally made by burning the previous year's palm leaves.
Lent to Pentecost, counted from Easter.First Sunday of Lent: Lent's 40 days exclude Sundays, which is why the season begins on Ash Wednesday, 46 days before Easter.
Lent to Pentecost, counted from Easter.Laetare Sunday: Meaning 'rejoice', this midpoint of Lent is a pause in austerity, and some churches replace purple vestments with rose-colored ones.
Lent to Pentecost, counted from Easter.Palm Sunday: It recalls Jesus's entry into Jerusalem, and many churches hand out palm fronds, which are later burned to make Ash Wednesday ashes.
Lent to Pentecost, counted from Easter.Maundy Thursday: The name likely comes from the Latin 'mandatum', or commandment, and many churches wash feet in memory of the Last Supper.
Lent to Pentecost, counted from Easter.Good Friday: Christians mark the crucifixion, and in many countries it's a public holiday, despite the name's 'good' puzzling many learners.
Lent to Pentecost, counted from Easter.Easter Sunday: Easter's date shifts each year because it follows the first Sunday after the first full moon on or after the spring equinox.
Lent to Pentecost, counted from Easter.Ascension Day: Always a Thursday, it marks Jesus's ascent into heaven and is a public holiday in countries such as Germany and France.
Lent to Pentecost, counted from Easter.Pentecost: The name comes from the Greek for 'fiftieth' and celebrates the Holy Spirit's arrival, often called the 'birthday of the Church'.
